name: Shreyanasanatha
role: Eleventh Tirthankara of the present age
summary: Shreyanasanatha is the eleventh Jain Tirthankara, said to be born at Simhapuri, identified with Sarnath. A rhinoceros marks his images.
about: Jain texts count Shreyanasanatha as the eleventh Tirthankara of this descending age. He is said to have been born at Simhapuri, identified with Sarnath near Varanasi, to King Vishnu and Queen Vishna of the Ikshvaku family. According to a Jain legend, a beautiful royal throne was thought to be haunted until his mother sat on it unharmed; the child was then named "lord of the good". He ruled a kingdom, became a monk, gained omniscience and taught non-violence and the shedding of karma (nirjara). Hemachandra places the Vasudeva Tripristha in his age, and Jain accounts count Tripristha as an earlier birth of Mahavira. Jains believe Shreyanasanatha was liberated on Mount Shikharji. His images are golden and have a rhinoceros on the pedestal.
kidSummary: Shreyanasanatha is the eleventh Tirthankara. A Jain story says a throne was thought to be haunted until his mother sat on it safely, so he was named "lord of the good". A rhinoceros marks his statues.

story.title: A throne no one dared sit on
story.text: Jain tradition says King Vishnu had a lovely throne that people thought was haunted, so no one dared to sit on it.

story.title: The brave queen
story.text: The queen sat on it, and nothing harmful happened. People felt the fear had been lifted.

story.title: Lord of the good
story.text: Her son was named Shreyanasanatha, which means "lord of the good".

story.title: Prince to monk
story.text: He grew up in Simhapuri, near Sarnath, and ruled for a while. Then he became a monk, and Jains say he gained perfect knowledge.

story.title: Teaching nirjara
story.text: He taught people to be non-violent and to let go of old karma through self-control. Jains believe he reached liberation on Mount Shikharji.

facts.text: A Jain legend says a royal throne was thought to be haunted, until his mother sat on it safely; the child born afterward was named "lord of the good".
A rhinoceros is carved on the base of his images. A 20th-century study of Jain iconography links it to the bold behaviour the legend gives the mother and child.

He is said to have been born at Simhapuri, identified with Sarnath, which is also famous for the Buddha's first sermon. Singhpur village, about 1.7 km northwest of Sarnath, is believed to be the spot, and Jains say four of his five great events happened there.

Jain accounts count Tripristha, a Vasudeva and younger half-brother of the Baladeva Achala, as the nineteenth birth of Mahavira's soul. The two brothers had different mothers but were inseparable as children.
Hemachandra says Tripristha's name means "three backbones", because the king saw three ridges on his infant son's back.
The Digambara Jain temple at Sarnath, built in 1824 and dedicated to him, stands only about 70 metres southwest of the Dhamek Stupa, so a Jain and a Buddhist shrine sit side by side.
Jainpedia says his Prakrit name, Sejjamsa, is explained by his mother's pregnancy craving to climb a precious bed (sejja). Another reading of the name is Sanskrit shreyas, meaning better or superior.
After a two-day fast he broke it at the house of King Nanda in the town of Siddhartha, then wandered for two months and gained omniscience under an ashoka tree, says Jainpedia.
Svetambara sources name his parents Vishnuraja and Vishnu; Digambara sources name them Vimalavahana and Nanda. Same Tirthankara, different parent names.
The Svetambara temple at Hiramanpur, Sarnath, was built in 1801 at the urging of the monk Jinakushalachandra-suri. A black stone image of him was installed in a Sarnath garden on 20 January 2005.

quiz.q: Which modern place is Simhapuri identified with?
Whose earlier birth do Jain accounts say Tripristha was?
quiz.why: Jain accounts count Tripristha as the nineteenth birth of Mahavira's soul.
Nirjara means shedding or discharging karma.
